item.title: IBM at NeurIPS 2026
item.description: NeurIPS runs December 6 to 12 in Sydney, with satellite locations in Atlanta and Paris. Here's where to find IBM, and what to ask us about Granite.
item.content:encoded:
Draft content

This post is draft content for review. Event details are from IBM at NeurIPS 2026. Granite-specific sessions aren't confirmed yet; we'll add them here when they are.

NeurIPS 2026 is almost here. The conference runs from December 6 to December 12, 2026, with the main event in Sydney, Australia, and satellite locations in Atlanta and Paris. IBM is returning as a Platinum sponsor and is presenting work at all three locations.

Find us at the booth​

Visit IBM booth #73 from Monday, December 7, through Thursday, December 10. The booth has demos across IBM Research, including foundation models, trustworthy AI, natural language processing and understanding, knowledge and reasoning, AI automation, human-centered AI, and federated learning.

Papers and sessions​

IBM's accepted papers, talks, and workshops will be listed on the IBM at NeurIPS 2026 page as the schedule is published.

Talk to us about Granite​

If you're attending, these are good conversation starters:

  • LLMON, the markup language that helps models tell instructions from data. See LLMON: teaching Granite to tell instructions from data.
  • Granite.build, for running LLM pipelines from a single build.yaml. See Granite.build: one file from model download to evaluation.
  • Your use case. Tell us what you're building with Granite and what you'd like to see next.

Can't make it?​

Follow along on the IBM at NeurIPS 2026 page, and join the conversation in Granite GitHub Discussions.

item.title: Granite.build: one file from model download to evaluation
item.description: An open source build orchestrator for LLM pipelines. Describe the pipeline once in build.yaml and run it locally, on Kubernetes, or on cloud GPUs.
item.content:encoded:
Draft content

This post is draft content for review. Facts are from the Granite.build README. Granite.build is in alpha, and breaking changes may occur.

Fine-tuning a model usually means a pile of scripts: one to download the base model and data, one to train, one to evaluate, and glue to move artifacts between them and between machines. Granite.build replaces the glue with a single pipeline definition.

Describe the pipeline once​

A Granite.build pipeline lives in a build.yaml file. It declares which models to download, how to fine-tune them, and which evaluations to run, as named targets such as download, fine-tune, and evaluate. Targets are connected through artifact bindings: when a target produces an artifact, the targets that depend on it are dispatched automatically.

Artifacts are addressed by URI, so the same pipeline can pull a model from Hugging Face with hf:// and write results to local files, Git, or cloud object storage (file://, git://, cos://).

Run it anywhere​

Each step runs in the environment you choose, without changing the pipeline:

EnvironmentStatus
Docker and local BashStable
KubernetesStable
SLURM through SkyPilotBeta
RunPod and SkyPilot on AWSBeta

The environments, credentials, artifact stores, and step implementations available to a build come from a space, so moving from a laptop to a GPU cluster is a configuration change.

The pieces​

  • gbserver, the orchestration server, with a REST API and a web dashboard. It watches for pending builds and dispatches them.
  • gb, the command-line client, to submit builds, check status, read logs, and manage artifacts.
  • Lineage tracking, which records where every build, target, and artifact came from.
  • Standalone mode, which uses SQLite and threads, so you can try everything without any external services.

Built to work with coding agents​

Granite.build ships Agent Skills for coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenCode, so an agent can operate the tool without being taught each time. The gbmcp MCP server lets agents start the backend and run, monitor, and cancel builds. The dashboard also has a chat assistant that only proposes actions: nothing runs until you approve it.

Try it​

You need Python 3.11 or later, plus Node.js 20 or later and yarn for the dashboard. Start the server in standalone mode:

git clone https://github.com/ibm-granite/granite.build.git
cd granite.build
make venv PYTHON=python3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
make build-frontend
gbserver standalone --space-dir configurations/spaces/local

Then, in a second terminal, submit the quickstart build. It runs a single step in a local Bash process, so no Docker is needed:

cd granite.build
source .venv/bin/activate
export GB_ENVIRONMENT=STANDALONE
gb build start -f samples/standalone/standalone-quickstart/build.yaml
gb build status <build-id>

The dashboard is at http://localhost:8080. For everything else, see the Granite.build repository, which is open source under the Apache 2.0 license.

item.title: LLMON: teaching Granite to tell instructions from data
item.description: Two new preview models learn a simple rule from an LLM-native markup language. Only the instructions you point them at are commands; everything else is input.
item.content:encoded:
Draft content

This post is draft content for review. Facts are from the LLMON announcement of November 12, 2026.

Every prompt is a mix of things you trust and things you don't. Your system prompt and instructions sit next to retrieved documents, pasted emails, and tool results, and to the model it is all one stream of text. Today we're releasing two experimental Granite models that see that stream differently.

The problem: everything looks like an instruction​

When an instruction is hidden inside a document or a tool result ("ignore the above and…"), a model can follow it as if you had written it. That is indirect prompt injection, and it gets more dangerous as models read more untrusted content on their own, in RAG pipelines and agents.

Formats like JSON don't help much. As the announcement puts it, JSON "was designed for parsers, not for causal language models": the brackets and quotes that mark its structure also appear in ordinary text, so the model can't reliably tell where one part ends and the next begins.

What LLMON is​

LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "lemon") is a markup language for talking to LLMs. It wraps each part of a prompt, such as an instruction, a document, or a requirement, in a tagged block. The delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so markup can never be confused with content:

<|open|>instruction<|close|>
  Suggest a title for the following email:
<|open_end|>
<|open|>data<|close|>
  Dear customer support, I am writing about the wifi on my recent flight...
<|open_end|>

An exec block then says which instruction runs on which data, much like a function call. Blocks that the exec block doesn't point to are still in context, but the model treats them as input to read, not commands to follow.

You rarely write LLMON by hand. The models' chat template renders ordinary chat messages into LLMON, and Mellea converts its LLM calls automatically.

What we released​

  • Granite 4.1 3B LLMON preview and Granite 4.1 8B LLMON preview, fine-tuned from the Granite 4.1 base models under the Apache 2.0 license
  • The LLMON toolkit with converters and example notebooks
  • An attention visualization Space that shows how the model's attention follows LLMON blocks

How well it works​

On the OPI prompt injection benchmark, the LLMON models avoided 47% more attacks than the best frontier model and 95% more than the best open-source model. On standard benchmarks, they perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models, so the added robustness doesn't cost general capability. The announcement has the full results.

What it doesn't do (yet)​

These are previews, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production. The separation between instructions and data is a learned behavior, not a guarantee, and the benchmarks above cover static, single-turn injections. Attacks that unfold over many turns are still being worked on, so keep your other safeguards, such as Granite Guardian, in place.

Try it​

  • Start with the LLMON concept page in these docs for an overview and links.
  • Run a model from its model card, which has a complete prompt example.
  • Read the research: the LLMON language paper and the post-training paper.

Tell us what worked, what broke, and which use cases you'd like to see in GitHub Discussions.
